newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor says Liberia must have elections in May.
newsitem.headline: Taylor says Liberia must have elections in May.

text.p: Former guerrilla leader Charles Taylor, who plunged Liberia into a brutal seven-year civil war, is now primed for May elections and has issued a veiled threat if they are delayed.

Taylor said on Saturday night any attempt by Liberia's donors or the United Nations to shift presidential and legislative elections from next May as scheduled under peace accords could trigger a crisis.
"Our side will find it virtually impossible to accept that elections cannot happen in May," Taylor told Reuters.

"We want to make it very clear that we have demonstrated our ability to fight a war, disarm our people and demobilise them. They should now give us the opportunity to hold elections," he said in an interview.
To hear Taylor, his victory in the presidential poll is a foregone conclusion. He has transformed his National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL) which launched the civil war.

Taylor's campaign machinery is gathering steam after he bolted from the starting blocks well ahead of other faction leaders. His Kiss FM radio and a party newspaper ensure his name is constantly in the news.

Taylor's name has been a household word since he started the war, and many Liberians admire his gritty, charismatic style. But it is hard to gauge his chances at the bollot box with many potential challengers not yet in campaign mode.

Many Liberians say Taylor squandered much of whatever goodwill he had by spearheading warfare in Monrovia last April and May that shattered the city just as Liberia finally looked truly headed for peace.
"I will vote for any civilian but not Taylor or any of the faction leaders. I can't forgive him for the destruction of Monrovia and all the warlords are the same," one Monrovia resident said.

Disarming guerrillas, the most important condition for peace and until now the most trecherous, appears to be on schedule -- exceeding expectations of both the United Nations and the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG.

Latest ECOMOG figures showed close to 25,000 guerrillas or well over 70 percent of armed men had turned in their weapons by a Friday deadline for voluntary disarmament. Taylor says more than 90 percent of his NPFL had demobilised.

But proposals for free and fair elections prepared by the United Nations and backed by donors and some foreign electoral experts, if adopted, could delay the polls beyond May. They deal with the composition of a new electoral commission, registration of voters and the use of proportional representation.
"Everybody knew about the schedule of implementation we signed. If there is deception involved that means that everything is changed," Taylor said.
"I can tell you this much. When you begin to change things and schedules and plans, you open up a pandora's box. There is a possibility and even a probability of crisis."
Taylor says Liberia should be treated as a special case so elections can go ahead while there is momentum for peace. He does not dispute he is in a hurry to be president.

Taylor's NPFL launched a civil war from neighbouring Ivory Coast on Christmas Eve of 1989. He came close to taking the capital in 1990 and 1992 but was thwarted on both occasions by the Nigerian-led ECOMOG force sent to Liberia in 1990 by the Economic Community of West African States.
